entries.title: Woman in custody after girl, 7, fatally stabbed in Chatham
entries.summary: <p>A 7-year-old girl died after being stabbed in the Chatham neighborhood Saturday, police said.</p><p>Edi Mari Hernandez Chacon was walking outside in the 8600 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue just before noon when a woman approached her and stabbed her multiple times in the back, according to Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Bystanders who witnessed the stabbing intervened and detained the woman, police said.</p><p>The girl was taken to Comer Children's Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.</p><p>The woman, who has not been identified, suffered injuries during the scuffle with bystanders, and she was transported to the hospital before being taken into police custody.</p><p>Detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Illini stunned at home by Boilermakers
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Freshman kicker Jacobo Echeverria Lozano booted three field goals and Antonio Harris scored a late touchdown on a 1-yard run as Purdue defeated Illinois 24-17 Saturday in a Big Ten Conference game.</p><p>Lozano was perfect from 30, 34 and 33 yards, making him 11 for 12 for the season, as the Boilermakers (2-3, 1-1) won in Champaign for the first time since 2022 and brought the Cannon Trophy home after losing to Illinois the past two seasons.</p><p>Purdue’s Ryan Browne was 18-for-27 passing for 255 yards and a TD. Assad Waseem caught three passes for 98 yards and Fame Ijebol rushed for 65 yards on 19 carries.</p><p>Katin Houser completed 21 of 37 for 225 yards and two TDs for Illinois (2-3, 0-2). Collin Dixon caught 10 passes for 116 yards and a score.</p><p>Ka’Lil Valentine, Illinois’ leading rusher, left the game in the first quarter with a right leg injury and did not return.</p><p>Down 13-0, Illinois scored on an 11-yard pass from Houser to Dixon with 21 seconds to go in the first half. It was Dixon’s eighth TD reception this season at Gies Memorial Stadium, extending his Illinois record.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Illinois: All eyes were on the Illinois defense after former defensive coordinator Bobby Hauck and head coach Bret Bielema mutually agreed last weekend following a 42-19 loss to No. 7 Ohio State that Hauck should resign. The unusual 3-5-5 defensive scheme that Hauck installed at Illinois was plagued by serious communication issues between players and coaches during the ex-Montana coach’s four-game tenure. The communication was better and so was the defense, but the offense was shut down most of the game.</p><p>Purdue: Purdue’s defense was the worst in the Big Ten coming into the game. It gave up 139 points in consecutive losses to Wake Forest, No. 23 UCLA and No. 3 Notre Dame. When Illinois’ Ethan Moczulski missed a 32-yard field goal in the second quarter, it was the first time this season the defense stopped an opponent from scoring inside the red zone. The second time was with 13 seconds left in the third quarter when Wisdom Sims knocked down a fourth-down pass from the Purdue 17.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Illinois: At Michigan State on Saturday.</p><p>Purdue: Hosts Minnesota on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' disastrous opening trip ends with late loss to Sabres
entries.summary: <p>BUFFALO, N.Y. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>’ disastrous season-opening road trip culminated with a 4-3 loss to the Sabres on Saturday.</p><p>It was easily the Hawks’ most competitive effort of the trip, given they carried a lead into the third period, but their long list of glaring problems appears far from fixed.</p><p>Jiri Kulich scored the Sabres’ game-winning goal with less than seven minutes left after Patrick Kane turned the puck over deep into a four-on-four shift and the Hawks never got locked in defensively. The Hawks haven’t won in Kane’s hometown since 2019.</p><p>"We started off playing the way we wanted to," Alex Vlasic said. "We need to do a better job of just maintaining that level of compete and speed and detailed hockey throughout the course of the game."</p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill reunited basically the same forward lines he had deployed throughout training camp — only to change them right before this trip — and that might've helped a little with chemistry.</p><p>Teuvo Teravainen, Anton Frondell and Tyler Bertuzzi, for example, connected on a beautiful tic-tac-toe goal in the first period.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Blackhawks have their second real highlight — the other being Patrick Kane's goal in Vegas — of the season: <a href="https://t.co/DFYk5hHfFn">pic.twitter.com/DFYk5hHfFn</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2106527582024089855?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks still seem structurally broken when it comes to limiting transition attacks, though, as the Sabres' 37-19 advantage in scoring chances belied.</p><p>Too frequently, all three Hawks forwards pushed too deep in the offensive zone and failed to force turnovers, leading to all three chasing the play as the Sabres raced the other direction on four-on-two rushes. Blashill said the Hawks talked about their "F3" positioning between periods, and it did seem to improve somewhat.</p><p>The Hawks’ defensive-zone coverage, puck support on defensive-zone breakouts and passing accuracy when trying to break out remain issues, too.</p><p>"I thought our compete and swagger was way better," Blashill said. "That’s more the standard that we want to play with. Obviously you’re going to make mistakes, and you want to learn and grow. That’s what we’ll focus on."</p><h3><b>Byram with family</b></h3><p>New Hawks defenseman Bowen Byram missed the game — which would've pitted him against his Sabres teammates for the last three years — while attending to a family matter, Blashill said.</p><p>Byram's wife, Kailey, posted on Instagram in July that the couple was expecting twins this fall.</p><p>Byram struggled in his first two Hawks games while handling huge workloads (about 25 minutes each), prompting Blashill to move Byram back to his natural left side halfway through the Mammoth game. The Hawks remain optimistic Byram will elevate their defense once he gets settled.</p><p>Byram's absence allowed both Kevin Korchinski and Ethan Del Mastro to slide into the lineup as a pairing while Sam Rinzel sat out. Blashill made it clear after the game that he liked Del Mastro's performance better than Korchinski's.</p><h3><b>Hello, Crevier</b></h3><p>Former Hawks defenseman Louis Crevier, part of the trade package for Byram, decided to sign a four-year contract extension with the Sabres before playing any regular-season games for his new franchise.</p><p>"It's just nice to know where I'm going to play for a long time," Crevier said.</p><p>The towering Quebec native was not only beloved by Hawks fans but also by Hawks teammates, coaches, staff, reporters and broadcasters — basically by everyone — so there were many warm greetings exchanged Saturday morning.</p><p>Crevier's eagerness to shoot — which the Hawks know well — paid off for the Sabres in the second period when Tage Thompson tipped in Crevier's shot to tie the game 2-2.</p><h3><b>Odelein passes</b></h3><p>Former Hawks defenseman Lyle Odelein died Friday. He was 58.</p><p>Odelein played 77 games across parts of two seasons (2001-02 and 2002-03) with the Hawks near the end of his long career. He won a Stanley Cup with the Canadiens in 1993 and later served as the first captain in Blue Jackets history.</p>

But that’s only a guess. Like most people who encounter Peace Prophet, Fullam knows little about her past and how she came to be homeless.</p><p>Peace Prophet lives with a mental illness, her family says. A conversation might begin with her asking if you’d like to buy a piece of her art and then rambles into a monologue of how she once starred in a film with Hollywood actor Lloyd Bridges and is, in fact, soon on her way to Los Angeles for the Academy Awards. Or how her family originally came from the Moroccan city of Marrakesh.</p><p>None of which turns out to be true. Details of her earlier life — both tragic and inspiring — came to light in early August, when a family member stumbled upon a <a class="Link" href="https://www.google.com/search?sca_esv=9690ff17f276db6e&sxsrf=APpeQnvUrFu0rSsDy3XF362MyuvomCODGw:1790879839438&udm=vids&fbs=ABfTbFVyMZGZf1hfvX9uKjN_-G8c4u0nXx4bEIpwm1lnNH832VTJOOCxW_fyN-Q_ezyf8gKjm3rhh_G8jdZ2Q6tji4z8GVSvqyGdykqk6W5STIO7Ee71YxW2VggeXfxXsifX2acu9faz9nqKXxdvTFDCNcPca2o8YQpxB3HvXbOQ0nbgsVmSIZl8bkKucbfjX5hqynpAoquyu_X6HR479h-ybDtmqV0ROA&q=peace+prophet+and+Geri+biamonte&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjYzqilu5mXAxXUiCsGHb_DOv4QtKgLegQIFhAB&biw=1382&bih=730&dpr=2#fpstate=ive&vld=cid:9dd601ce,vid:S9GwjSU82eo,st:0" target="_blank" ><u>YouTube</u></a> talk about Peace Prophet and then reached out to the lecturer.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>* * *</b></p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"></p><p>Chances are, if you even occasionally head downtown, you have seen Peace Prophet. She’s as much a fixture outside of the State Street Macy’s as the smartly dressed Jehovah’s Witnesses proffering copies of “The Watchtower” magazine. Those who don’t know Peace Prophet’s self-chosen name may still know her as, say, “the homeless artist lady.”</p><p>Because that’s what she does. She paints. She draws. Constantly — like a fish that must keep swimming to stay alive.</p><p>“I am drawn to people who express themselves unabashedly,’” says Nick Cappelletti, a Saugatuck, Michigan, art gallery owner who has sold Peace Prophet pieces for about the past five years.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>* * *</b></p><p>I first searched for Peace Prophet back on a chilly morning in early May. I had just seen her work for the first time at the Intuit Art Museum, an institution in West Town devoted to self-taught artists. Over the next four months, I wanted to understand where she came from, why she lives on the streets and the source of her creativity.</p><p>Trying to find Peace Prophet can feel like chasing shadows. </p><p>“I saw her yesterday,” says a clerk at a downtown Staples, where she often gets free paper.</p><p>Try the Dunkin’ Donuts in the subterranean Chicago Pedway, someone else suggests.</p><p>No luck.</p><p>“She’s been on the street for 20 to 30 years because I’ve been selling StreetWise since 1993. Homeless as a jaybird,” says Lester Cherry, a vendor hawking the weekly magazine outside Macy’s. She is best known for her portrait sketches and photo-booth selfies, which she often daubed with paint or ink.</p><p>There has been a groundswell of public support in recent years for self-taught art and artists, but it’s still not given the respect it deserves, Bonesteel says.</p><p>“Even today, there is a strong institutional bias against it from people who are trained. There is a kind of veiled bigotry toward it,” he says.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>* * *</b></p><p>One day in June, Peace Prophet is in the basement of Blick’s, bent over a drawer filled with sheets of art paper. She buys three, handing the cashier two crumpled dollar bills. She heads back out onto the streets.</p><p>Is she available to chat?</p><p>“I don’t have time today. I’m waiting for someone,” she says brusquely.</p><p>Who?</p><p>“My daughter.”</p><p>Peace Prophet paints, to the accompaniment of a wailing police siren, the rumble of a passing L train and a chorus of drills biting into concrete.</p><p>An hour later, the white paper is awash in vibrant color — a Black woman with a wide-brimmed hat, resembling a Nigerian churchgoer in her Sunday best.</p><p>There is no sign of Peace Prophet’s daughter.</p><p>But as it turns out, the daughter is no figment of her imagination. Peace Prophet has four children, all grown, and eight grandchildren. They know her as Janice Carol Rivers, born at the old St. Luke’s Hospital in the South Loop on July 30, 1955, according to Cook County Clerk’s Office records.</p><p>Peace Prophet’s remarkable story begins to trickle out in late July after her son found on YouTube a talk Biamonte, the UIC social worker and collector, had given in 2019 about the artist and her work.</p><p>The son shared his discovery with his siblings. “We were blown away. Our mom has struggled with mental illness our entire lives. … I haven’t seen her since 2024,” Peace Prophet’s youngest daughter writes in a July 13 Facebook message to Biamonte.</p><p>Janice Rivers was a quiet, serious child who, to hear her only surviving sibling describe it, was born with a paint brush in her hand.</p><p>“She was always painting, drawing, coloring,” says the brother, born James, but who later converted to Islam and now goes by Hakim Abdul-Ahad and lives in Las Vegas.</p><p>In the family’s yellow-brick Woodlawn apartment, Janice kept an easel, she stretched her own canvases. She devoured books about Picasso, Van Gogh, her brother says. She listened to French language instruction on old 45 rpm records.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a She felt like I wasn’t on her side,” Gaia says.</p><p>Gaia’s father, who died in 2007 of complications from heart disease, would eventually gain full custody of all four of his children, moving them to suburban Willowbrook. Gaia says she was a sophomore in high school and on her way to a homecoming dance when she visited her mother at a local hospital. There, doctors told the family that the patient had bipolar disorder, which causes alternating bouts of mania and depression.</p><p>Peace Prophet took medicine for a time, but hated the way it made her feel, her daughters say — and so she stopped. Her illness seized control. She bounced from apartments to a group home and, eventually, to the streets in the year 2000, Gaia says.</p><p>“She just left and that was it,” Gaia says. “She was gone.”</p><p>That left Gaia to fill the mother void for her three much younger siblings when she was still in high school; even so, she is not bitter.</p><p>“Given that it was beyond her control, I couldn’t really be mad at her,” Gaia says.</p><p>Peace Prophet’s youngest, the musician, says all the children are affected in different ways by their mother’s absence.</p><p>“The pain that I feel about her is more so about the fact that I’m sure at 25 years old, she never thought she was going to be a homeless lady at 70,” she says. “It just makes me sad thinking about all that she’s missed out on.”</p><p>The family has tried many times, the daughter says, to give Peace Prophet a better life. They searched all day, went to a night club, then finally found their mother at 3 a.m., curled up inside the revolving door of a downtown bank.</p><p>“We didn’t know for sure it was her. We were like, ‘Hey Mom.’ … Somebody started unzipping the bag, and she poked her eye out and it was her,” the daughter says.</p><p>Their mother’s connection with strangers through art is welcome but bittersweet, the daughters say.</p><p>“This is amazing that so many people love her art. But it made me sad. I know in her mind right now she’s not fully capable of understanding how much people love and enjoy her art,” says Tina, the middle daughter, who works as a phlebotomist and lives in Burr Ridge.</p><p>The youngest daughter has a theory about the woman who appears so often in Peace Prophet’s work, the one with the sidelong glance.</p><p>“It’s depicting her mental illness in a drawing,” she says. “The way the person is always looking off [to the side], to me it’s encapsulating paranoia, always looking over your shoulder.”</p><p>Others have said the woman in the painting illustrates the way many people treat the homeless: unwilling to look them directly in the eye.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>* * *</b></p><p>It’s Lollapalooza weekend, and streets across from Grant Park teem with glittered-up, flesh-baring youth. It’s a bad day to try to find Peace Prophet. But it’s her birthday. She’s 71 years old. Her youngest daughter, the L.A. musician, wants to wish her a happy birthday, something she has never done.</p><p>The daughter, reaching out from Los Angeles, asks if the Sun-Times can take a phone along with us to make that happen. We are happy to help.</p><p>Peace Prophet is nowhere to be found. We make four loops of her typical stomping grounds, head underground, resurface. We’re about to give up when we see a sweater-clad woman on the north side of the State Street Macy’s. It’s her. She’s holding up a painting, still wet, that looks like stalks of fresh lavender laid out on a table.</p><p>“We have a surprise for you,” I say.</p><p>Peace Prophet looks at the cell phone and at the young African-American woman and child huddled on the screen.</p><p>She peers closer. The armor of distrust falls away. She smiles — a wide, toothy grin.</p><p>“I love you, Mommy. I hope you have a good birthday today,” the daughter says.</p><p>“I’m doing this art thing, hustling around,” Peace Prophet says.</p><p>She isn’t sure how old she is today, maybe 69, 39, 80.</p><p>“You’re 71,” her daughter says.</p><p>Then Peace Prophet’s granddaughter begins to sing, her voice piercing the roar of traffic and the pedestrian chatter just a few feet away.</p><p>“Happy birthday to you, happy birthday, Grandma Janice, happy birthday to you!”</p><p>Peace Prophet stares transfixed at the screen and then says, in a whisper, “I love you.”</p><p>Still holding up the painting she hopes someone will buy today for a few dollars, Peace Prophet declares: “It’s the best birthday I ever had.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Alina Edwards</i></p>

entries.title: How NHL's salary boom affects Blackhawks' negotiations with 2027 restricted free agents
entries.summary: <p>The NHL contractual environment in which the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> are now operating has never before looked like it does now.</p><p>Salaries for superstars are skyrocketing, as are the long-term salary-cap projections. The cap is now projected to jump to $127.5 million in 2028-29, marking a 53% increase in just five years (since 2023-24).</p><p>General managers have responded with an increasing willingness to make sizable commitments — in terms of both term and salary — to unproven young players, just to get them locked in at semi-reasonable cap hits and avoid the extreme boom scenarios. </p><p>Sportsnet's Elliotte Friedman has <a class="Link" href="https://www.sportsnet.ca/nhl/article/32-thoughts-dawn-rises-on-a-new-nhl-after-summer-of-change/" target="_blank" >termed</a> this 2026-27 season as "Year 1 AC — After Carlsson," referring to Ducks forward Leo Carlsson's whopping offer sheet this summer that ignited this salary boom. It's clever, and true.</p><p>Ducks GM Pat Verbeek has certainly changed his ways dramatically since the bombshell, if the $43.2 million contract he just gave defenseman Tristan Luneau (boasting all of 14 games of NHL experience) is any indication.</p><p>And Hawks GM Kyle Davidson has been awed by the speed of change as much as anyone. He shared some fairly unfiltered thoughts about it Tuesday in Las Vegas.</p><p>"The Leo Carlsson contract certainly felt like a little bit of — or a lot of — a land shift," Davidson said. "We didn’t see that coming. You hear rumblings, but you hear rumblings every year on stuff like that. It changed things, and you have to crank the dial a little bit and figure out what this new world means — and try to stay ahead of it, to some extent.</p><p>"It’s just the nature of it. These things happen, and you have to react. You can’t be stuck in the past in many respects because you’ll be...left behind. I think we did alter our thinking a little bit and got some contracts in. </p><p>"But I think it’s a constant adjustment. The pendulum seems to have swung. I don’t know if that will swing back or if it'll keep pushing out. It remains to be seen."</p><p>In Oliver Moore's case, the Hawks decided it worthwhile to act quickly. Despite having seen just 60 NHL games of the speedy forward, they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/24/blackhawks-oliver-moore-contract-nhl-salary-cap-cost-certainty" >signed him</a> to a five-year contract with a $4.25 million cap hit before this season began. </p><p>If Moore busts, he'll be overpaid. But if he breaks out for, say, 50 points this season, he would have been much more expensive to sign as a restricted free agent next summer.</p><p>"Sometimes you get into conversations and there’s traction and it just culminates in a deal," Davidson said. "A lot of times, it doesn’t and you kick the can down the road. This one did. It’s a combination of us really believing in the player and...he loves being a Blackhawk. He wanted to commit."</p><p>That's one pending 2027 RFA down and four notable ones left for the Hawks. Forward Ryan Greene and defensemen Artyom Levshunov, Sam Rinzel and Wyatt Kaiser all fall in that bucket, too.</p><p>If unsigned by July 1, Kaiser will have arbitration rights coming off his second contract, but the other three — coming off their entry-level deals — will not.</p><p>Davidson said he has "had some soft conversations the last little while" with those players, adding he's "always open to doing something."</p><p>That's only if the price is right, though. And it makes sense why the Hawks might not feel as much urgency to get pen to paper in those situations.</p><p>Greene, while a smart and reliable player, doesn't seem likely to boom into a major point producer, which caps his realistic salary potential. The same could be said of Kaiser.</p><p>On the other hand, Levshunov and Rinzel certainly have high upside and genuine boom potential, but they've been extremely inconsistent in the NHL so far. The Hawks might want to be more careful accumulating data on them before doing anything audacious.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/24/blackhawks-oliver-moore-contract-nhl-salary-cap-cost-certainty" >Blackhawks get cost certainty on Oliver Moore’s new five-year contract</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Comments about granddaughter's weight put grandma in the doghouse
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I moved 2,000 miles to be near my daughter and her family. One of my granddaughters, "Libby," was diagnosed with a medical condition and has put on some weight. I was at my daughter's and was going to mention my concern for my granddaughter's weight. Before I could finish, my son-in-law came in, told me I shouldn't be talking about Libby's weight and walked away. I thought I could talk to my daughter about things I was concerned about. I left feeling very hurt.</p><p>I sent a text to my daughter apologizing. My son-in-law came to my house and said I need to filter what I say. He then told me I have made remarks to my grandchildren that hurt them. I love my family with all my heart. I would die for them. Was I wrong to mention my concern about Libby? I'm devastated that my daughter didn't come to talk with me about it. Am I wrong? — <i>MEANT WELL IN IDAHO</i></p><p><b>DEAR MEANT WELL:</b> It is disappointing that your son-in-law had to come and talk to you rather than your daughter. Talk with her, and ask how you can interact with her and her family more positively.</p><p>It is generally known these days that weight is a sensitive subject, particularly if it is associated with a medical condition. If Libby is under a doctor's care, you can be confident that everything that can be done for her is being done. Because you have now been informed that some of the comments you have made have hurt your grandchildren, it may be time to close your mouth and turn on your "listening ears" when you visit. Also, when you want a private conversation with your daughter, make sure that it is, indeed, private.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have known "Ralph" for many years and consider him one of my best friends. We share many interests, and through the years we have frequently discussed them over the phone. Ralph retired recently and is bored, so now he calls me three or four times a week, even when there is nothing new to talk about. We rehash the same things over and over again. I've dropped subtle hints that my life doesn't change much from day to day. If I allow his calls to go to voicemail, he leaves a message and asks me to call him back. I don't want to be rude, but how can I get him to call less frequently? — <i>DUCKING CALLS IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DUCKING CALLS:</b> If Ralph's voice message doesn't contain a reason for you to call him back, you're not obligated to do so with any urgency. It's not rude of you to enforce a waiting period between your calls with him.</p><p>Whenever he does bring up a worn-out topic, say something like, "Oh, yeah, we talked about this a few days ago!" Then immediately change the subject. In this way, you subtly make it obvious that you're not going to let him drag you into the same conversations time and time again.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
